summary: Taken together, items 1-5 are the classical four-dimensional Dehn invariant: its definition, the ridge-sum formula, invariance under scissors congruence, and its use to separate the regular 4-polytopes. Hadwiger and Jessen established this theory in research papers, and it has a clear specialist audience in scissors congruence and polytope valuations, where Jessen's theorem shows it is complete in dimension 4. The literature account is careful and honest about its limits. It cites the main sources, discloses which ones were not read, claims no new invariant, and makes only a modest absence claim about the table of six invariants. The dihedral angles, the irrationality argument and the relation θ_600 = 4π/3 − θ_5 all check out.

internal_notes.message: Dihedral angles checked: arccos(1/4) ≈ 75.52°, 90°, 120°, 120°, 144°, and arccos(−(1+3√5)/8) ≈ 164.48°, which equals π/3 + arccos(−1/4). θ_600 = 4π/3 − θ_5 holds exactly. x = −(1+3√5)/4 is a root of 4x² + 2x − 11, so 2cos θ is not an algebraic integer and θ_600 is not in ℚπ. The 5-cell argument (2cos θ = 1/2) is also correct. The claim that the two non-zero invariants are opposite multiples of one rank-one tensor is correct.

The submission handles item 5 honestly. It restricts claims to the pairs that actually differ and says that the zero-invariant polytopes are not separated. It says correctly that Jessen's theorem gives the converse at equal volume, and that this converse is not proved in the entry. This is positive evidence for the literature account.

Attribution of completeness in dimension 4: Encyclopedia of Mathematics credits Jessen 1972 (pp. 47-53, MR 0353150) with the four-dimensional results. Wikipedia credits completeness in four dimensions to Dupont and Sah (1990). The submission names both ("Jessen proved; Dupont and Sah later gave proofs through group homology"), but gives no exact citation for the Dupont–Sah paper (Acta Math. 164 (1990) 1–27). Jessen 1972 is disclosed as read only through citations. This is a minor bibliographic gap, not misattribution.

Hadwiger introduced the higher-dimensional invariants, and the submission does not cite him; it mentions 'Hadwiger's higher invariants' only in the prior-formalization search. Jessen 1968 is cited for the higher-dimensional tensor form, so the classical source for invariance (item 3) is partly covered. I could not confirm whether Hadwiger or Boltianskii already stated that the regular n-simplex is not scissors congruent to the n-cube for n ≥ 3. With no affirmative evidence, this is not a finding. A valuations survey (arXiv:2302.00416, seen only in a search snippet) gives a dimension-general argument that a regular simplex is not scissors congruent to a cube. This suggests the 5-cell part of item 5 is a known special case, which fits the submission's own 'classical' framing.

Lagarias–Moews published an 'Acknowledgment of Priority' (DCG 14 (1995) 359–360). The likely prior work is Debrunner (1980) on space-fillers, which Wikipedia cites alongside Lagarias–Moews. I could not read the note's text. Lagarias–Moews is context only, not part of the claimed results, so this is not material.

The abstract of arXiv:1101.3833 (Zakharevich, scissors congruence as K-theory) does not itself state that completeness is known in dimensions 3–4 and open in dimension ≥ 5. That statement is standard and appears on Wikipedia; it may be in the paper's body, which I did not read. Minor.

The submission reports a search of Lean, AFP, Coq/Rocq, HOL Light, Metamath and Mizar that found no 4D Dehn invariant. I found nothing that contradicts this, but I did not repeat the search across every system.

Notability rests on the classical theory: Hadwiger's higher-dimensional invariants and Jessen's 4D completeness theorem. The audience is research mathematicians in scissors congruence (group homology, K-theory: Dupont, Sah, Zakharevich), valuations and polytope theory. The table and the non-congruence corollaries alone would be routine exercises. The case for notability depends on items 2–3 being the genuine ridge-sum identity and the full invariance theorem for finite unions, not something weaker.

Pre-score of a proposed entry: there is no Solution, Challenge or Comparator configuration yet. The coverage manifest above lists the planned statements in place of declaration names. A real review must check that the Lean statements match items 1–5. It must check in particular that dehnSet4 is not defined so as to force the ridge-sum identity, and that the bridge covers finite unions with common refinement as stated.

what_would_reach_higher: Cite Hadwiger, 'Zum Problem der Zerlegungsgleichheit k-dimensionaler Polyeder', Math. Ann. 127 (1954) 170–174, as the classical source of higher-dimensional invariance (the classical counterpart of item 3). Check whether it, or Boltianskii's 'Hilbert's Third Problem' (1978), already proves that the regular n-simplex (n ≥ 3) is not scissors congruent to the cube; if so, credit it for the 5-cell part of item 5.

Cite Dupont and Sah exactly: 'Homology of Euclidean groups of motions made discrete and Euclidean scissors congruences', Acta Math. 164 (1990) 1–27. Read at least the passage in Dupont's 2001 book or Sah's 1979 book that states Jessen's 4D theorem, so the completeness attribution rests on an inspected source rather than on citations of Jessen 1972.

Add Debrunner (1980) next to Lagarias–Moews for the space-filler context, and note their 1995 Acknowledgment of Priority, or drop the Lagarias–Moews sentence as not needed for the theorems (it does not support the claimed results).

Check that arXiv:1101.3833 actually contains the 'complete in dimensions 3 and 4, open in dimension ≥ 5' statement attributed to it, or attribute that statement to a source that does (Dupont's book or Wikipedia's sources).

Strengthen notability: state the ridge-sum identity and the bridge for the full class (finite unions of convex 4-polytopes, every hyperplane cut, every affine isometry). Name the research audience explicitly in the README (scissors congruence and K-theory, valuations), with one line on why a set-defined invariant matters, for example as a step toward Jessen's 4D sufficiency theorem or Hadwiger invariants in all dimensions.

A higher reach: prove the general-n version (the codimension-2 Dehn invariant is a scissors-congruence invariant in every dimension n ≥ 3). Or prove one direction beyond invariance, such as the Hadwiger-style statement that every regular n-simplex (n ≥ 3) is not scissors congruent to the n-cube. Either would raise the result above an extension of the 3D entry to one more dimension.
